Really wanted to like this movie but just couldn’t :/ All the characters were one dimensional. I’m also unable to be invested in a “flawless,” holier than thou, Christ-esque main character. Felt I had zero stake in what happened because of this. Generally there were too many characters and species to really understand them or be invested in them. I also didn’t like the art. One of my favorite parts of studio Ghibli movies is the animation. Whether whimsical, artsy, or beautiful, I’ve always been impressed by the animation. This movie lacked all the usual charm and beauty. I found the plot similarly underwhelming. I love a good save/respect the environment from human greed story as much as the next liberal, but this one was lackluster. I’m not a fan of the unquestionable regard for the gods theme. This lack of critical thinking and respect merely for power is exactly what led the townspeople to blindly follow their gun-wielding woman leader. That being said the ending was kinda sorta satisfying and I did cry over a damn pig 💀

I made the grave mistake of watching this movie dubbed instead of subbed, so I won’t hold this too much against it, but the voice acting was some of the absolute worst I’ve ever seen. Princess Mononoke in particular was clearly just reading lines in a random room with 0 direction. The score was pretty memorable, and the animation is good as always obviously, but that’s about all I can say for this movie’s positives. This movie was rated PG-13 but it was clearly made for 3 year olds. The reason I claim this is because the themes are so childish and immature that it immediately breaks immersion and makes taking this movie seriously impossible. Hate causes war and humans cause war and war is bad and nature is good. Gee whiz, what an original and compelling concept. The dialogue in this movie was horrific. This is an ANIMATED FUCKING MOVIE, yet this movie ONLY TELLS, AND NEVER SHOWS. There is a scene where a character literally says “the night walker turns into the forest spirit when daylight comes, look! It’s doing it now!”. Hey fucking dumbfuck, do you realize this is an animated movie? And I have an IQ score above 35? And I’m not a toddler? SHOW MEEEEEEEEEEE!!! YOU DONT NEED THIS DIALOGUE YOU CAN JUST SHOW ME. I’m so sick and tired of Japanese animation movies treating me like a dumbass. I am a human being, I have emotions such as empathy, and I have body parts such as eyeballs. You do not need to tell me what the character is feeling, and a character doesn’t need to describe to me what he is seeing, because I have a heart, and I have eyeballs. The exposition dumping too, holy shit is it irritating and plentiful. This (animated) movie establishes that this is a fantasy world with unique mechanics which exist within it, but rather than showing us, the characters just do a full exposition dump every single scene because you are 3 years old and cannot infer anything. Everything must be spoon fed to you. The plot of this movie is stupid. I am so sick and tired of human beings making movies about how humans ruin nature. Whether I agree or disagree with it, it is such a tired, boring concept. The main character gets a “hate virus” (very subtle) and then it kinda manifests into nothing and also the main character is basically like a perfect human being with 0 flaws and also when he is told he’s gonna die he doesn’t even have a reaction. All of the characters wanna kill each other, but there’s not a single memorable character in the movie so who cares. I don’t care about any of them because the movie gave me no reason to. One thing I will say is at least this movie was thought provoking. Not with anything regarding humans vs nature or love vs hate, but it did get me thinking, how are you supposed to rate movies that you feel are 1-4/10? I want to rate this movie higher because it has aspects like the animation and the score that are good, but the reality is, 5 minutes into the movie I was already rolling my eyes and begging for it to end, so what do I rate this? I’m gonna go with 3/10 I guess, because I truly hated it. I find it infinitely puzzling how when it comes to gaming, Japanese developers are consistently pioneers in challenging their player base, but when it comes to movies/TV, it feels like there’s are made for people who have bird brains and couldn’t possibly figure anything out by themselves unless it’s shoved down their throats.

Acho que eu fui com muitas expectativas, assisti esse logo após ter assistido “Túmulo dos Vagalumes”, então imaginem como a expectativa estava alta. O enredo do filme é baseado em vingança e dá pra entender os dois lados da história. É errado pensar que era só todo mundo ter aceitado viver em paz, porque todos sabemos que não é assim que a banda toca, senão não teríamos guerras. Mas sei lá, faltou profundidade na Princesa pra mim. Gostaria de ter visto o retorno do Ashitaka para a aldeia dele, nem que fosse só pra explicar tudo que aconteceu. Também queria ter visto mais do convívio dele com a princesa. Será que no final o pessoal da refinaria e da floresta de fato conseguiram viver em paz? Em nenhum momento eu consegui odiar completamente a princesa ou a Lady Eboshi, porque o filme faz questão de mostrar que as duas têm suas razões. E acho que essa foi a parte que eu mais gostei ninguém ali é totalmente bom ou totalmente mau. Mesmo assim, terminei com a sensação de que queria saber muito mais sobre eles e sobre o que aconteceu depois. Talvez eu tenha ido esperando sentir o mesmo impacto que senti com Túmulo dos Vagalumes e simplesmente não aconteceu. Não achei ruim, mas esperava muito mais.

"Life is suffering. It is hard. The world is cursed. But still, you find reasons to keep living." Really shocked about how much my thoughts have shifted on this film. But, I just cannot get behind what this film is trying to say with it's main character. Ashitaka is a fence sitter, his whole purpose is to stop the war between the genocidal rageful humans, and nature that is simply trying to live and exist in a world slowly being taken over by human rage and desire for control, by peaceful means, we should make peace with our oppressors and be nice to each other. San is a character I actually love. She breaks free from the confines of the narrative, by the end she is the same she still hates humans and will probably continue to protect her home. But, unfortunately the film paints this as something bad throughout the film. I do appreciate this film not doing the common trope of the male character changing the female character, and then falling in love with each other for no reason so that's something, I guess. Overall it's a shame I don't love this film as I once did but this is probably the most disneyfied Ghibli movie I've seen so far.

Princess mononoke is about man vs nature. The old world vs the new one. With the rise of industrialisation animals have been displaced and the lands have been desecrated. Our hero doesn’t only have to cure himself from a curse of hatred but he must also heal a world that is full of war and bloodshed. And restore nature to what it once was. Lady eboshi is a nuanced figure she is a symbol of feminism, a saviour for the sickly, a successful businessman in the development of iron and yet she is also a person who violates the lands and the animals within it. Her ambitions for building a civilisation come at a cost of the balance of the lands. She is in a long line of people whose aspirations are to conquer land and reshape it in their image. Her internal contradictions are compassion vs malice. Ashitaka is someone who is also conflicted his curse wants vengeance while his soul yearns for peace. Princess mononoke is someone who is fighting for the old world she is less a human and more a wolf loyal to her pack. She is traditional while lady eboshi is more modern. Mononoke is also nuanced while fighting for the land she places it above the value of human lives. Ashitaka is someone who sees both sides he’s a mediator of sorts he’s balanced. Understanding the value of both man and nature. He seeks to end the cycle of hatred. His relationship with mononoke is interesting for the first time she cares about a human and is cared for by one. The forest spirit is the epitome of nature. Nature doesn’t fight back it simply exists. The animals are the ones who fight for their land. Natives fighting invaders. The forest spirit is a god who gives life and takes life. It is an enigmatic figure who is peaceful. But the story isn’t just about man vs nature but also man vs man. Fighting for land in senseless wars. Clawing for power. An emperor who desires immortality and is willing to kill nature to get it. Jigo at first seems like a nice man yet he ends up being an antagonist someone who does his emperors bidding. Everyone in the story is morally grey. There are no absolutes the film isn’t black and white it’s much more than that. When the spirit of the forest dies its body dissolves and liquid starts to spread draining the life of everything it touches. The universe has been disrupted and chaos is the result of humanity’s ambitions. This film speaks to humanity’s greatest feats and at the same time its worst atrocities. In the end Ashitaka returns the spirits head and restores the land. This suggests the idea of renewal is a real possibility. And if we allow it nature can remain a beautiful and sacred place. Humanity must learn to coexist with nature without letting progress destroy it.

Hot take: this movie is overrated. I had high expectations, and I agree that it's a beautiful animated film, but I find myself not engaging with it much. The narrative felt tedious and convoluted for a bit. The whole time I was watching the last arc of the film, I thought, "When is this going to end?" I couldn't get behind the characters, as I think that they're one-dimensional and flat (except Lady Eboshi). Maybe San's enigmatic characterization was intentional; it just seems to me that she was underutilized, her dilemma was made minuscule compared to that of other characters, and there's no "completion" to her arc. For a titular character, she was underdeveloped, as was her romance with Ashitaka. Another one of my gripes with this film is that the affair between Ashitaka and San was forced, dry, and uninteresting. It was sudden, no buildup, no chemistry at all. I would say that the film's strength lies in its ethics: the non-dichotomous conflict between humans and nature, and the message that humans should coexist with nature. I just hoped I was invested in the characters, so I felt underwhelmed at the end.

Sadly this marathon went out with a whimper. I was hype to watch this one, I heard it was a little more action heavy and that sounded nothing like the previous 6 movies we watched. I was then highly disappointed by JUST HOW MUCH EXPOSITION IS IN THIS LIKE SERIOUSLY WTF. The pace at which they throw this at you is insane and I really struggled to care about anyone in the end because just so much dialogue is just pure, unfiltered exposition. This got in the way of character chemistry, the overall development of the plot, the pacing and removed any subtlety from the themes this film tried to address. If you can ignore the poorly pace plot and severely underdeveloped characters (aside from maybe Lady Eboshi), this films presentation and atmosphere were beautiful af. Just in the first 25 minutes alone, I could tell how much media took inspiration from it (from BOTW to even Dark Souls). The 2.5 stars are solely due to just how good this movie looks man like it’s actually crazy, cinematic as hell. My sister and I came away from this one disappointed, it absolutely didn’t help that Pop needed help waking up from a nightmare by the end it… not a good look for the film.

“Forest Spirit, we give you back your head!!!!!!” Watching a Myozaki film makes me feel dead inside. I know that sounds a little hysterical but let me explain. ‘Princess Mononoke’ (like Miyazaki’s entire oeuvre) exudes creativity. The animation is extraordinary, there’s an unparalleled level of narrative imagination and the music is phenomenal. ‘Princess Mononoke’ is an objectionably good movie. But to me, the picture was about as interesting as ‘Fern Gully.’ I think it comes down to one’s tolerance of spirituality. Not religion, spirituality. I have very little. The second someone starts babbling about the spirit of the forest, I check out. I took a trail run today and all I saw was poison ivy and a dead raccoon. You combine the spiritual babbling with the ‘uncanny valley-esque’ dialogue and I am put right to sleep. Not sure why Studio Ghibli gets a pass for their garbage dubbing. To its credit, ‘Princess Mononoke’ starts with a bang. The demon boar set piece is incredible. I was getting ‘Legend of Zelda’ vibes through the first 20 minutes, not to mention a surprising level of violence. I was fully on board. But soon enough we are bombarded with all sorts of twee-ass bullshit and character arcs that feel random at best. That’s about it. I don’t want to sit here and shit on something created with such an obvious level of care and intention. As I’ve said before, I needed to experience Miyazaki as a kid before I was such a cynical asshole. Nostalgia is a hell of a drug, just wait for my ‘Pollyanna’ review. I think I’ve come to the realisation that I find it incredibly hard to emotionally invest myself in anime or ghibli films that are completely based in fantasy worlds, whether it be Howl’s Moving Castle, Akira or… this. Or maybe it’s just a coincidence. Spirited Away worked for me because it thrusts an everyday child into a fantastical situation, and we get to live that wonderment through their eyes. With Princess Mononoke, I couldn’t help but feel a disconnect, some kind of restraint. I’m not entirely sure. I just didn’t care for anybody or anything. Even though I thought the characters were incredibly well written, with in depth opinions and alibis. I want to care! Please!! I’ll give this some of the benefit of the doubt for now as I will give this a rewatch eventually, when I can take it in on my own with no outside distractions. But by no means did I not enjoy it though. I loved the landscapes, character designs, the pacing. Attributes of which I admittedly found easier to appreciate than I usually do. All working in tandem, all making for some undeniably gorgeous filmmaking. And the score, goddamn, Miyazaki never fails to add a few tracks to my playlist.

"Eu te amo, Ashitaka. Mas nunca perdoarei os humanos." Apesar de um ritmo arrastado e de uma tremenda falta de conexão com as personagens, Hayao Miyazaki ainda consegue debater temas relevantes que me fazem perguntar como alguém pode ter plena convicção de que animação é coisa de criança. Dos conflitos entre as próprias tribos, que retratam essa falta de unidade e como, muitas vezes, se perde de vista quem são os verdadeiros inimigos, até grupos completamente marginalizados encontrando seu espaço na sociedade. A obra questiona que tipo de sociedade é essa que, ao mesmo tempo em que acolhe, também é capaz de causar tanto dano. Vale a pena estar incluso nela? Um filme que, mesmo com todas essas nuances, não cai no conto da falsa equivalência. Porque nem todo conflito é formado por dois lados de uma mesma moeda. Às vezes, existe apenas um lado tentando resistir enquanto o outro avança sob um discurso dito “progressista”. Se uma animação do século passado ainda consegue retratar questões tão atuais, talvez o “progresso” não tenha nos levado tão longe assim. Se sobressai sobre tudo o que assisti dele até aqui, mas está longe de ser, para mim, essa obra prima que tantos pintam por aí.

I had an extremely hard time following this movie as so many of the intricacies are so context based and not explained, which I understand is a Japanese cultural difference and it’s sort of my fault for not being able to follow along, but I genuinely think that getting a deeper dive into who the characters were and what the world was at the beginning of the movie and not just throwing you into the story would’ve made the whole thing easier to follow and enjoy without having to change anything else. So that’s really my only complaint, but definitely more of a personal thing. Now that I’ve seen it once and understand, I wouldn’t really want anything changed for a rewatch, and I would totally enjoy watching it again. I think this is one of the most relevant movies I could’ve decided to watch at this time, as I’ve been pondering the exact dilemma in the message. As I’ve been studying international relations and history more deeply, I know that the question of survival between two parties when one side’s existence is dependent on the other not existing is a very prevalent issue throughout history and resurfacing now. And the hatred personified by the demons is the true standout. When humanity is stuck in this dilemma, the most blinding force is a grueling hatred that engrossed people to ignore the obvious environmental clues, like Okkoto blinded to the scouts by the demon, reminding me of the Israel-Palestine conflict. How can both exist, and especially with this hatred? It’s a very relevant message that I think everyone should see. I just wish it were easier to follow so that the message can be driven home more clearly, because I believe that most people (myself included initially) will see this movie and think that it’s just about protecting the environment, and how industrialism etc. and our desire to obtain “everything between heaven and hell” and play god is creating this war between us and nature. Of course that message is true, but it fits into the more encompassing and more important overarching theme I mentioned.

OUR COMPLICATED RELATIONSHIP WITH  NATURE  AND OUR OWN HUMANITY This was my first time watching Princess Mononoke, and I was amazed by how beautifully the film was made and how Hayao Miyazaki brought his imagination to life. It is truly one of Studio Ghibli’s masterpieces, and I would place it as my second favorite Ghibli film, after Spirited Away. The film explores several social issues, but I think its central theme revolves around war, a recurring subject in Hayao’s work. It shows how destructive war can be and how innocent people and other species are dragged into senseless and inhumane conflicts. It also explores how vengeance fuels conflict, suggesting that as long as hatred persists, wars may never truly end. I loved how the film portrayed the destructive effects of human greed and selfishness, not only on nature and other species but also on humanity itself. One of the most interesting aspects was how animals were portrayed as beings capable of hatred and vengeance. They were not simply helpless victims; their desire to defend themselves could eventually evolve into rage, making them capable of hurting humans as well. The animation was exceptional, and the depth and artistic detail of each creature were truly remarkable. The film was also filled with metaphors and symbolism that required close attention. My only criticism was that the ending felt somewhat rushed, leaving me wanting clearer closure. I also feel that I need to rewatch it to fully appreciate the symbolism and details I may have missed. Overall, Princess Mononoke is a visually stunning and thought-provoking masterpiece that explores war, vengeance, greed, and humanity’s complicated relationship with nature.

La princesa Mononoke es una de esas películas que parecen sencillas hasta que uno empieza a mirar debajo de la historia. A primera vista podría parecer un relato sobre la lucha entre los humanos y la naturaleza, pero reducirla a eso sería perder prácticamente todo lo que la hace especial. Miyazaki construye una historia sobre la industrialización, la guerra, el progreso, la marginación, el odio, la espiritualidad y la convivencia, pero sin convertir ninguno de esos temas en una respuesta fácil. Lo más interesante es que no existen buenos y malos absolutos. Los humanos están destruyendo el bosque, sí, pero no porque todos sean crueles o quieran destruir la naturaleza por simple avaricia. Lady Eboshi es el mejor ejemplo. Es quien impulsa la explotación del bosque y quien quiere acabar con los dioses que se interponen en el camino de Iron Town, pero también es una mujer que cree sinceramente que está construyendo un futuro mejor para su gente. Ha creado una comunidad donde personas rechazadas por la sociedad encuentran un lugar. Las mujeres de Iron Town son especialmente importantes. Eboshi las ha sacado de los burdeles y les ha dado trabajo y una cierta independencia, convirtiéndolas en parte esencial de la producción de hierro. También acoge a hombres afectados por la lepra, personas profundamente marginadas en la sociedad de su época, y les permite trabajar y recuperar una dignidad que otros les habían negado. Resulta paradójico que una mujer capaz de ofrecer libertad y protección a personas marginadas sea, al mismo tiempo, responsable de una destrucción enorme del mundo natural. Y precisamente ahí está la grandeza de Eboshi: no es una villana que sabe que está haciendo el mal. Cree que está haciendo lo necesario. Quiere hierro, armas, territorio y seguridad para su ciudad. Quiere que Iron Town prospere. Su problema no es simplemente la maldad, sino la convicción de que el progreso humano justifica conquistar aquello que se interpone en su camino. La película se sitúa, además, en un Japón que está dejando atrás un mundo antiguo. Ashitaka pertenece a los Emishi, un pueblo prácticamente desaparecido ante la expansión del poder imperial. Iron Town representa una nueva época: el hierro, la industria, las armas de fuego y una sociedad que empieza a dominar la naturaleza mediante la tecnología. El bosque, en cambio, pertenece a un mundo anterior, espiritual y ancestral. La película convierte ese cambio histórico en un conflicto entre formas distintas de entender el mundo. Pero Miyazaki tampoco idealiza la naturaleza. Los dioses y animales del bosque son capaces de amar, proteger y sacrificarse, pero también están llenos de rabia. Nago, el dios jabalí, es herido por una bala humana y su dolor se transforma en odio hasta convertirlo en un demonio. Esa misma maldición acaba alcanzando a Ashitaka. Su brazo se vuelve monstruosamente fuerte cuando actúa movido por la ira, pero esa fuerza también lo consume. Es una de las metáforas más bonitas de la película: el odio puede darte fuerza y destruirte al mismo tiempo. Los jabalíes representan precisamente esa tragedia. Quieren recuperar lo que los humanos les han arrebatado, pero su deseo de venganza acaba cegándolos. Okkoto, viejo y orgulloso, termina recorriendo un camino parecido al de Nago. La película deja claro que el sufrimiento de la naturaleza es real, pero también que el odio puede corromper incluso a quienes han sido víctimas. Y ahí aparece Ashitaka. Ashitaka es probablemente el personaje más importante porque no intenta decidir quién merece ganar. Cuando llega al conflicto, intenta comprender a ambos lados. Su filosofía queda resumida en una frase que dice en japonés: 曇りなき眼で見定め、決める。 Kumori naki manako de misadame, kimeru. Algo parecido a: «Ver con ojos despejados, discernir y decidir». La conocida traducción «ver con ojos libres de odio» captura el espíritu de la idea, aunque no sea una traducción literal. Ashitaka intenta mirar sin permitir que el odio, el miedo o los prejuicios decidan por él. Eso es exactamente lo contrario de lo que ocurre con casi todos los demás personajes. San odia a los humanos porque siente que han destruido el mundo al que pertenece. Es humana, pero fue abandonada de niña y criada por Moro, por lo que considera a los lobos su verdadera familia. No quiere volver a la sociedad humana y no necesita hacerlo para que su historia tenga sentido. Ashitaka la ama sin pedirle que abandone aquello que es. Moro, por su parte, sabe que los lobos están perdiendo la batalla y que su propia vida se acerca al final. Sin embargo, continúa luchando por San y por el bosque. Su relación con ella también habla de una idea muy hermosa de la familia: no hace falta compartir sangre para pertenecer unos a otros. Y después está Shishigami. Quizá sea el elemento más difícil de interpretar porque Shishigami no representa simplemente a «la naturaleza». Es algo mucho más profundo. Es la vida y la muerte al mismo tiempo. Da vida, cura y mata. No es bueno ni malo porque la vida misma tampoco funciona bajo esas categorías. Su forma de ciervo durante el día y su gigantesca forma nocturna, el Daidarabotchi, parecen mostrar distintas dimensiones de una misma fuerza. Cuando pierde la cabeza, la vida se convierte en destrucción y todo aquello que toca muere. Cuando finalmente recupera su cabeza, la vida vuelve a brotar. Y aquí llega uno de los momentos que más sentido le da a toda la película. San observa el bosque después de la muerte de Shishigami y dice que ya nunca volverá a ser el mismo. Ashitaka le responde, en esencia, que Shishigami es la vida misma y que, por tanto, la vida continuará. No significa que todo vaya a volver a ser como antes. De hecho, no volverá. El bosque ha sido destruido. Iron Town también ha quedado devastada. Los dioses han sufrido. Personas y animales han muerto. El mundo anterior ha desaparecido. Pero aparecen pequeños brotes. La vida continúa. Y esa es quizá la idea más hermosa de toda la película: la naturaleza no necesita regresar exactamente a lo que era para estar viva otra vez. Por eso el final no es una victoria de la naturaleza sobre los humanos. Tampoco es una victoria humana sobre los dioses. Es una reconstrucción. Ashitaka decide quedarse cerca de Iron Town y ayudar a reconstruirla. San permanece en el bosque. No se «salvan» mutuamente convirtiéndose en personas diferentes. Se quieren, pero respetan que pertenecen a mundos distintos. Es una conclusión sorprendentemente adulta: amar a alguien no significa obligarlo a convertirse en aquello que tú quieres que sea. También por eso Jigo resulta tan interesante. Frente a Eboshi, que realmente cree en su proyecto, Jigo representa el oportunismo. Entiende que el mundo está cambiando y simplemente quiere beneficiarse de ello. Para él, incluso la cabeza de Shishigami puede convertirse en un objeto de poder y riqueza. Es la transformación definitiva de algo sagrado en algo que puede poseerse. Y esa es otra de las grandes tensiones de la película: cuando los humanos dejan de mirar la naturaleza como algo que forma parte de ellos y empiezan a verla exclusivamente como un recurso. El hierro sirve para fabricar herramientas y construir una comunidad, pero también armas capaces de matar a un dios. El progreso puede liberar a unas personas y destruir a otras. La tecnología no es presentada como algo malvado; lo que importa es la relación que establecemos con ella. Por eso La princesa Mononoke no pide que volvamos a vivir sin tecnología ni que abandonemos el progreso. Tampoco dice que los humanos debamos desaparecer para que la naturaleza pueda vivir. Propone algo mucho más difícil: aprender a convivir sin convertir al otro en un enemigo que debe ser eliminado. Al final, Ashitaka no consigue eliminar el conflicto. No consigue que San ame a los humanos, ni que Eboshi deje de construir, ni que el bosque vuelva a ser el que era. Lo único que consigue es impedir que el odio sea la única respuesta posible. Y quizá esa sea la verdadera razón por la que la película sigue siendo tan poderosa. Porque habla de un mundo en el que todos tienen motivos para luchar y, precisamente por eso, todos pueden terminar destruyéndolo todo. Los humanos quieren sobrevivir. El bosque quiere sobrevivir. San quiere proteger a su familia. Eboshi quiere construir un futuro para la suya. Los jabalíes quieren recuperar lo perdido. Los marginados quieren simplemente tener un lugar donde vivir. Nadie está completamente equivocado y nadie está completamente a salvo de equivocarse. Y en medio de todos ellos está Ashitaka, intentando hacer algo aparentemente sencillo pero extraordinariamente difícil: mirar con ojos despejados antes de decidir. Porque La princesa Mononoke no trata realmente de escoger entre humanos y naturaleza. Trata de preguntarnos qué ocurre cuando dejamos que el miedo, el odio y el deseo de poseer algo nos impiden ver que el otro también está intentando sobrevivir. Y, sobre todo, nos recuerda que aunque destruyamos el mundo que conocíamos, mientras exista vida siempre queda la posibilidad de empezar a construir otro. El bosque ya no será el mismo. Pero está vivo.

Não tem muito o que discutir aqui, Hayao Miyazaki simplesmente pegou tudo aquilo que torna o cinema do Studio Ghibli especial e levou para um nível absurdo. É um filme emocionante, inteligente, lindo e narrativamente complexo, capaz de contar uma história de fantasia gigantesca enquanto discute questões muito reais sobre natureza, humanidade, violência e equilíbrio. O mais impressionante é que "Princesa Mononoke" não trata seu conflito central como uma disputa simples entre o bem e o mal. Não existe um lado completamente certo e outro completamente errado. Humanos destroem a natureza, sim, mas também precisam sobreviver. Os espíritos da floresta são fascinantes e poderosos, mas também podem ser perigosos. Cada personagem possui suas próprias razões, e Miyazaki desenvolve seu roteiro afim de compreender essas motivações. O filme consegue falar sobre preservação ambiental sem transformar sua mensagem em um discurso moralista de duas horas. A natureza não é apresentada como algo simplesmente bonitinho que precisa ser protegido porque sim. Ela é poderosa, imprevisível e muitas vezes assustadora. Ao mesmo tempo, os seres humanos não são tratados como uma praga sem salvação. Existe bondade mesmo nas pessoas responsáveis por causar parte daquele conflito. San também é uma personagem maravilhosa justamente porque não pode ser resumida à palavra "princesa". Ela é feroz, determinada e ligada à floresta, mas também é alguém que vive um conflito de identidade e pertencimento. Ashitaka, por outro lado, funciona como uma ponte entre mundos completamente diferentes. Ele não está simplesmente procurando derrotar alguém, está tentando compreender um conflito no qual praticamente ninguém consegue enxergar o outro lado. Miyazaki permite que seus personagens tenham motivos legítimos mesmo quando suas ações são destrutivas. Lady Eboshi, a principal antagonista da história, é o melhor exemplo disso. Ela pode estar contribuindo para a destruição da floresta, mas também oferece um lugar para pessoas marginalizadas e cria uma comunidade onde outras pessoas encontram dignidade. Como você simplesmente olha para uma personagem assim e coloca um adesivo escrito "vilã" na testa? Além disso, "Princesa Mononoke" é lindo em praticamente todos os frames. As florestas, os espíritos, os animais, as cidades, os cenários e até os momentos mais violentos tem uma identidade visual impressionante. Mas a beleza não está ali apenas para impressionar. A floresta é basicamente um personagem (literalmente e metaforicamente), e sua presença muda completamente dependendo do momento da narrativa. Miyazaki consegue fazer você enxergar beleza e ameaça no mesmo espaço, o que combina perfeitamente com a própria mensagem do filme. Não existe uma solução mágica capaz de apagar séculos de conflito para enfim encontrar a coexistência. Não basta destruir o inimigo e seguir em frente. A verdadeira resposta parece estar na tentativa de compreender aquilo que é diferente, mesmo quando essa compreensão não resolve tudo imediatamente. É uma mensagem extremamente humana escondida dentro de uma fantasia sobre deuses, guerreiros e criaturas gigantes. O filme possui momentos de violência e tragédia com muitos detalhes, mas nunca utiliza isso apenas para parecer adulto. As consequências importam. Quando alguém sofre, aquilo tem peso. Quando a natureza é destruída, existe uma sensação de perda real. Quando um personagem toma uma decisão, o filme permite que essa decisão tenha consequências reais. E é justamente por isso que considero esse um dos melhores filmes do Studio Ghibli. Ele possui toda a magia característica do estúdio, mas não depende dela para funcionar. Você pode assistir pela fantasia, pela animação, pelos personagens, pela ação ou pela beleza visual e ainda assim encontrar muito mais coisas escondidas por baixo de tudo isso. É um filme que recompensa tanto a criança fascinada pelo mundo fantástico quanto o adulto interessado nas ideias por trás dele.
